examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule
examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = \tan u, \qquad u = \sin x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \sec^2 u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = \cos x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we express

$$
f(x)=(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f={u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=2u\,\text{\style}font-family:inherit;\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =2u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$
